items.title: Why an unknown segment GUID gets 422 from the controller
items.body:
Follow the stages. The GUID is well formed, so binding succeeds: it becomes a real Guid. Validation checks shapes and simple relations (dates, sort names), so it passes too. The scope filter compares workspaces from the route and the key; those match, so no 403.

Only inside the controller does Harbor look the segment up in the caller's tenant. It is not there, so `BuildAsync` returns null, and the controller keeps the existing 422 ProblemDetails contract. The guide calls this case different from bad input: the ID has a valid shape, but the segment is not available in this tenant.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "404 from the scope filter": that filter only compares workspace IDs and answers 403; it knows nothing about segments.
- "400 from model binding": binding fails only for malformed values, and this GUID is well formed.
- "403 for another tenant": the route's workspace matches the key; the segment simply is not found in it.

excerpts.quote: A missing segment is different: its ID has a valid shape, but the segment is not available in this tenant. `BuildAsync` returns null and the controller preserves the existing 422 ProblemDetails contract.
Invalid dates and unknown sort names cannot bind correctly; an undefined numeric sort is rejected by enum validation.

items.title: A webhook receiver should deduplicate on a stable delivery ID
items.body:
Harbor can send the same webhook more than once. The receiver may accept it while Harbor never sees the reply, or Harbor may crash after sending and before saving the outcome; both lead to another attempt. So a receiver must recognise repeats.

It needs something that stays the same on every attempt of one delivery: a stable delivery identifier. The signing timestamp is not that, because the guide says it can change per attempt. The guide also explains what the other tools do: HMAC verification proves the body was not tampered with, and a timestamp tolerance limits replays of old requests; neither shows a delivery was never processed before.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "The HMAC signature": a signature covers the signed content including the timestamp, so it is not a stable ID across attempts; HMAC is for integrity.
- "Nothing, use the timestamp tolerance": tolerance limits old replays; a retry within the window gets through.
- "The signing timestamp": the guide says it can change per attempt.

excerpts.quote: The receiver may accept a request even if Harbor never observes the response. A crash after sending and before saving can cause another attempt.

Receiver deduplication should use a stable delivery identifier, not the signing timestamp, which can change per attempt. HMAC verification establishes integrity and a timestamp tolerance limits old replays; neither alone establishes that a delivery has never been processed before.
The signature covers "{timestamp}.{body}" rather than the body alone, and /// the timestamp travels in the header.

readMore.why: How Harbor signs and verifies each delivery.

items.title: Signed bytes must not change between publish and send
items.body:
The right answer: re-serializing when sending could alter the bytes and void the signature.

An HMAC is computed over exact bytes. If Harbor rebuilt the JSON at send time, any difference in property order, casing or formatting, for example from a change to how the API renders responses, would produce different bytes than a receiver expects for that signature. So the payload is serialized once at publish time with pinned options (`Webhooks.PayloadJson`) and those bytes are sent verbatim. The outbox stores the exact payload for the same reason.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Cheaper to store once": cost is not the reason the ADR gives.
- "Entities cannot be loaded after the save": nothing in the ADR says so; the issue is byte stability.
- "Receivers require camelCase": the ADR pins options so the bytes are reproducible, not to satisfy a receiver's naming rule.

excerpts.quote: never re-serialized at send time, which would change bytes and invalidate the signature.

items.title: A broken segment is rejected once, when it is written
items.body:
The right answer: on save, with a 422, from compiling its rules once at write time.

A segment's rules have to become SQL every time the segment is used. If a rule could not compile, every list or membership read would throw. ADR 0005 moves that failure to the moment of writing: saving a segment compiles its rules once, and a segment that does not compile is refused with 422. Reads then only ever see segments known to compile.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "On the first list read, as a 422": the check runs when the segment is written, so the bad rule never reaches a read.
- "On save, as a 400 from model binding": binding checks the request's shape; the rule problem is found by compiling it, and the ADR names 422.
- "On every read, as a 500": that is exactly the behavior the write-time check exists to prevent.

excerpts.quote: Rules are validated by compiling them once at write time, so a broken segment is rejected with `422` instead of throwing on every read.

items.title: Moving ToListAsync earlier keeps the rows but changes the cost
items.body:
Before the refactor, `Where`, `OrderBy` and `Take` were added to an `IQueryable`, so the database did the filtering, sorting and limiting and sent back only a few rows.

After moving `ToListAsync()` to the front, the query is executed right away with no filter, so every row of the table comes into memory. The later `Where`, `OrderBy` and `Take` still run, but now as plain in-memory LINQ over that list. The visible result can be identical, which is why this is easy to miss: the guide says moving ToListAsync earlier can keep the result while turning a bounded request into a full-table load.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Nothing changed, EF defers ToListAsync": ToListAsync is the call that executes the query.
- "Take fails after ToListAsync": Take works fine on an in-memory list; it just runs in the app.
- "Only SQL formatting changed": the SQL no longer contains the WHERE or the limit at all.

excerpts.quote: `ToListAsync` executes it and brings rows into application memory. Moving `ToListAsync` earlier can preserve the visible result while changing a bounded request into a full-table load.

readMore.why: Tests that check the SQL, not only the returned rows.

items.title: Test a deadline with exact times, not with sleeps
items.body:
Harbor's domain methods take a `now` argument instead of reading the clock themselves. That means a test can call the method with "now = exactly the deadline" and again with "now = one tick later" and check both answers. The result is exact and the same every run. The workshop recommends this: prefer exact values around a deadline over sleeping until a real clock crosses it.

A "tick" is far smaller than any sleep you could rely on. A sleep of 100 ms lands at some unknown point after the deadline, and how long it really takes depends on the machine. So the workshop asks you to explain why a 100 ms wait cannot establish a one-tick boundary.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Move the machine clock": that changes shared state outside the test and is not what the guide suggests; the clock is meant to be an input.
- "Run many times, accept a majority": a test that sometimes fails is not evidence of the boundary.
- "Sleep 100 ms past the deadline": this is exactly the approach the workshop says is unreliable.

excerpts.quote: Domain methods take `now`, allowing tests to choose exact times. The integration harness also lets fixtures pin timestamps directly. Prefer exact values around a deadline over sleeping until a real clock happens to cross it.
Explain why a test that waits 100 milliseconds cannot reliably establish a one-tick boundary.

readMore.why: The section "The clock is an input" on controllers that still read the real clock.

items.title: What the transactional outbox does and does not guarantee
items.body:
When a conversation changes, Harbor does not call the subscriber's server right away. `Webhooks.cs` adds a "pending delivery" row to the same database save. One save, one transaction: either the conversation change and its pending delivery both commit, or neither does. That removes the bad case "saved the conversation but crashed before queuing the event". This pattern is called a transactional outbox.

The subscriber's HTTP server is a different machine. The SQLite transaction cannot include it. Sending happens later, when a dispatcher reads the pending rows.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Exactly once delivery": the same guide shows retries and crashes can cause another attempt, so receivers must deduplicate.
- "The HTTP call is rolled back too": no HTTP call happens during the save, and an HTTP call could not be rolled back anyway.
- "Sent inline before SaveChangesAsync returns": the guide says Webhooks.cs does not send HTTP inline.

excerpts.quote: Harbor queues webhook deliveries in the same database save as the conversation or message change. [Webhooks.cs](../../src/Harbor.Infrastructure/Webhooks.cs) adds pending delivery entities; it does not send HTTP inline.
It does not make the subscriber's HTTP server part of the SQLite transaction.
A crash after sending and before saving can cause another attempt.

readMore.why: The decision record for the outbox.

items.title: A write to another workspace's resource is a 404 too
items.body:
The right answer: 404, because the workspace-scoped lookup finds no such contact for this caller.

By-id routes carry no workspace in the path, only an opaque id. Every resource query adds `c.WorkspaceId == User.GetWorkspaceId()`, so a contact in workspace B is invisible to a caller from workspace A, exactly like an id that never existed. ADR 0002 applies the same answer to writes: a PUT, like a GET, gets 404. Any other code would tell the caller that the id is real somewhere else, turning the status code into an oracle.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "403, refused not hidden": 403 is used for a foreign workspace in the route; for a by-id resource it would confirm existence.
- "403 for writes, 404 for reads": the ADR says writes also 404 rather than 403.
- "409 because another workspace owns it": a conflict response would leak the same existence information.

excerpts.quote: Writes to a foreign resource also 404 rather than 403, for the same reason.

items.title: Workspace bootstrap is anonymous because no key exists yet
items.body:
The right answer: it mints the first admin's key, so it must work before any key exists.

Every other workspace operation is authenticated with a teammate's API key. But a brand-new workspace has no teammates and therefore no keys. Something has to create the first admin and hand back that admin's key, and that request cannot present a key it does not have yet. ADR 0001 names `POST /api/workspaces` as that one bootstrapping path.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Workspace names are public": the ADR makes no such claim; the reason is the chicken-and-egg problem of the first key.
- "The mail relay calls it": the relay is only listed among the services that call Harbor; it has nothing to do with bootstrap.
- "Rate limiting per IP is enough": the ADR does not justify anonymity with rate limiting at all.

excerpts.quote: is anonymous and mints the first admin's key — the one path that must work before any key exists.

items.title: Segment membership is composed as a subquery, not a list
items.body:
The right answer: as a subquery over contact ids, so it stays a single SQL statement.

SegmentCompiler turns the segment's rules into an expression EF translates into a WHERE clause over contacts. The conversation filter then uses that contact query as a subquery (`SegmentQueries.ContactIdsQuery`), so the database evaluates membership and the conversation filter together, in one statement, however many contacts match.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Load the matching ids and pass them back in": this is the shortcut the Context rejects; the id list grows with the segment and needs a second query.
- "Filter the contacts in memory": also rejected; it works on ten contacts and falls over on a million.
- "Read a refreshed membership table": membership is live and evaluated against contacts as they are now, so there is nothing to refresh or invalidate.

excerpts.quote: not a materialized list, so it stays one statement however many contacts match.

items.title: Why List and Overview share one conversation query
items.body:
A filter like `state=Open&q=alpha` has to mean the same set of conversations everywhere. The guide calls that set membership: which conversations belong. Harbor keeps membership in one shared query component. Each controller action then decides what to do with that set: `List` adds ordering, tags and paging; `Overview` adds a SQL aggregate (the counts). Because both start from the same membership code, the two endpoints cannot quietly read a filter in two different ways.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "So EF can cache one query plan": the guide's reason is consistent meaning, not plan caching, and the two endpoints run different SQL anyway (a page vs an aggregate).
- "Infrastructure may not reference controllers": the guide does discuss layers, but to explain where the component lives (the API project, since its input is an API contract), not why it is shared.
- "So the overview can reuse paging and tags": the overview does not page or load tags; those are added only by `List`.

excerpts.quote: `List` adds ordering, tags, and paging. `Overview` adds a SQL aggregate. The shared component defines membership: which conversations belong in the result. Keeping membership in one place prevents two endpoints from accidentally interpreting a filter differently.
This component lives in the API project because its input is an API contract.

items.title: When the rows stay right, test the SQL itself
items.body:
The right answer: SegmentSqlTranslationTests, which assert the generated SQL text itself.

If segment filtering silently moved into memory, the endpoint would still return exactly the right conversations. Every ordinary functional test checks rows, so every one would still pass, while the query had quietly become a full load that falls over at scale. ADR 0005 therefore tests the property that changed: SegmentSqlTranslationTests calls `ToQueryString` and asserts that `json_extract` is present, the filter sits in the WHERE clause, and the conversation filter is a subquery.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "A latency budget": the ADR names no timing test, and small test data would hide the cost anyway.
- "A row-count assertion": in-memory filtering returns the right rows, so counts do not change.
- "The request log": the ADR does not use logs to detect this regression.

excerpts.quote: A regression to in-memory filtering would still return the right rows and pass ordinary functional tests

items.title: Harbor pages by default and clamps oversized page sizes
items.body:
The right answer: the first page of 50, then a page whose size is capped at 200.

ADR 0007 exists to make unbounded list responses impossible. So a caller that sends no paging parameters does not get everything: it gets the first page with the default page size of 50. Out-of-range values are clamped rather than rejected, so `pageSize=500` is capped at the maximum of 200, and a page past the end is simply empty. Only values that cannot be parsed at all, such as `?page=abc`, still produce a 400 from model binding.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Every matching row": returning everything when parameters are omitted is the hazard the ADR removes.
- "A 400 for pageSize 500": Harbor clamps instead of rejecting; it trades strictness for robustness.
- "A page of 500, the max is advisory": the maximum is enforced by capping.

excerpts.quote: a page past the end is an empty page, which is what a client walking pages expects; a `pageSize` over the max is capped.

items.title: Why the created-date window is half-open
items.body:
The guide gives the rule: `createdFrom <= CreatedAt < createdBefore`. The start is included, the end is not. That shape is called half-open. Its big benefit: windows placed end to end, like Jan 1 to Jan 2 and Jan 2 to Jan 3, neither overlap nor leave a gap. A row created exactly at midnight on Jan 2 belongs to the second window only. And both bounds describe creation time, not last activity.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Inclusive, with end-of-day 23:59:59.999": the guide warns against inventing a `.999` end of day, because the database can store finer precision, so rows in the last fraction of a millisecond would be missed.
- "Exclusive on both ends": then a row exactly on a shared boundary falls into neither window, a gap.
- "Last-activity time, truncated to the day": the guide says the bounds describe creation time, not last activity.

excerpts.quote: The new bounds describe creation time, not last activity:

createdFrom <= CreatedAt < createdBefore ``` Adjacent windows `[Jan 1, Jan 2)` and `[Jan 2, Jan 3)` neither overlap nor leave a gap. Avoid inventing an end-of-day timestamp ending in `.999`; the database can represent greater precision.

readMore.why: Workshop 2 lists the boundary values to test for a date window.

items.title: Core idea: a query is a description until something runs it
items.body:
In EF Core, an `IQueryable` is not a list of rows. It is a description of database work. Each `Where`, `OrderBy` or `Take` adds to the description, and some call eventually sends it to the database and brings rows back into memory. A useful question for every query in the guide is: where exactly is that call, and which operators come before and after it?

The same guide splits a list request into three separate jobs:

- **Membership:** which rows belong (the filter).
- **Order:** which comes first.
- **Page:** which slice of the ordered rows to send.

For each job, find the line in `ConversationQueries.cs` or `Paging.cs` that does it, note the order the three run in, and think about what the result would look like on a large, changing queue if that order were different. A good habit from the guide: print the SQL with `ToQueryString()` and find the workspace predicate, the ordering and the limit yourself.

excerpts.quote: An `IQueryable<Conversation>` describes database work. `Where`, `OrderBy`, and `Take` add to that description.
Use the debugger to read `sql`. Identify the workspace predicate, ordering, and
Goal: explain both a query's result and where its work happens.

readMore.why: The shared helper that counts, writes paging headers and returns one page.

items.title: What adding Id as a tie-breaker fixes, and what it does not
items.body:
Many conversations can share the same timestamp. If the sort only uses that timestamp, the database may return tied rows in any order, so the same page can contain different rows each time. Appending `Id` ascending gives every row a unique place: a total order. On data that is not changing, page 2 is then always the same rows.

It does not freeze a live queue. The guide is explicit: if a new row arrives before your current offset, the next page can repeat a row; if one leaves, a row can be skipped. A cursor or a snapshot deals with that, which is a different design choice.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "It freezes the queue": the guide says the opposite, in those words.
- "It turns offset paging into keyset paging": Harbor still uses offsets (`Skip`); the guide mentions keyset only as an alternative.
- "It only speeds the query up": the purpose is a unique, reproducible order, not speed.

excerpts.quote: Multiple rows can have the same timestamp. Harbor now appends `Id` ascending to each supported conversation ordering. Database pagination needs unique ordering;
This does not freeze a changing queue. If a new row enters before your current offset, the next page can repeat a row; if a row leaves, it can skip one.

readMore.why: Where the orderings and the Id tie-breaker are built.

items.title: What goes wrong if you filter after paging
items.body:
The right order is: filter (membership), then sort, then count and take one page. With 500 matches and page size 2, you get 2 rows and `X-Total-Count: 500`.

If the code paged first, it would take 2 rows from the unfiltered list and then filter those 2. Some or all of them may not match, so the page has too few rows (maybe zero). And whatever count you take at that point no longer describes the 500 matching conversations, so the total header is wrong too. The guide states both results: too few rows and the wrong total; counting after paging only counts that page.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Two rows and 500, just slower": the problem is wrong results, not only speed.
- "Same rows, different order": the rows themselves change, because the slice was taken before filtering.
- "A 400": page size smaller than the match count is normal paging, not an input error.

excerpts.quote: For a queue of 500 matching conversations, page size 2 should return two rows while `X-Total-Count` remains 500. Filtering after paging can return too few rows and the wrong total. Counting after paging answers how many rows are on that page.

readMore.why: ToPageAsync counts the filtered query first, then skips and takes.

items.title: Why the late human edit normally overwrites without a 409
items.body:
Harbor's version token works inside one server request. EF remembers the version it loaded, and when it saves, the update matches only if that version is still in the database. If another writer changed it in between, the save fails and the API returns 409.

But no version travels to the browser. When the first human finally submits, that is a brand new request. It loads the conversation fresh, with the colleague's latest version, applies the change and saves. The versions match, so the save succeeds and overwrites the colleague's edit. The guide says this new request normally loads the latest version, and that client-visible stale-edit protection needs a separate contract, such as conditional writes.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "409, because the browser sent its version": the guide says the API does not send an edit token to the browser at all.
- "It blocks until the other transaction closes": optimistic concurrency does not wait; it compares versions at save time.
- "EF merges field by field": EF raises a conflict on overlap; it does not merge edits.

excerpts.quote: EF compares the original token during the update; another writer changing it can cause `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`, which the API maps to 409.

It does **not** send an edit token to a browser and require it on a later request. If a human reads a page, another human edits it, and the first later sends an update, that new request normally loads the latest version.

readMore.why: Where the version changes when a tracked entity is modified.

items.title: Start here: Harbor is a practice backend; read the guides in this order
items.body:
Harbor is a small C# web API (support conversations, workspaces, webhooks) built for learning. The learning guides live in `docs/learning/`. This pack's questions come from five of them. Read them in this order:

1. `docs/learning/README.md`: what Harbor is, and the six-step way to use each session (predict, trace, change, verify, explain, record).
2. `request-tracing.md`: follow one GET request through identity, binding, the controller and the database.
3. `data-and-queries.md`: when a query runs, filtering vs paging, time windows, tie-breaking, safe arithmetic.
4. `testing-workshop.md`: what each kind of test proves and what it does not.
5. `reliability.md`: transactions, version tokens and retries.
6. `debugging-labs.md` when you want hands-on practice with the same ideas.

Keep the source files open beside the guides. The README's learning map names them, for example `WorkspaceScopeFilter.cs` for tenant boundaries and `Paging.cs` for paging. Each guide gives a claim and points to the code that makes it true; check the code rather than trusting the sentence. Use `glossary.md` whenever a word stops you.

excerpts.quote: 1. **Predict:** write down what you expect before running code. 2. **Trace:** locate the actual implementation and its nearest test.
| HTTP, binding, DI, tenant boundaries | [Trace a request](request-tracing.md) | `Program.cs`, `WorkspaceScopeFilter.cs`, `ConversationsController.cs` |

readMore.why: A guided first session if the repo feels too big.
Short definitions for the terms the guides use.

items.title: Why a foreign workspace gets 403 without a database lookup
items.body:
When the API key is checked, Harbor records the caller's workspace as a claim on the user. `WorkspaceScopeFilter` runs on every workspace route. It reads the `workspaceId` from the URL and compares it with that claim. If they differ, it answers 403 right there. It never asks the database whether workspace B exists. The code comment says the comparison never touches the database, so a 403 reveals nothing about whether the other workspace exists.

By-ID endpoints (one conversation by its ID) work differently: they look up ID and caller workspace together and return 404 when nothing matches.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Loads B first, then 403 or 404": that lookup would leak whether B exists; the filter deliberately avoids the database.
- "404 for every mismatch": the filter returns 403 Forbidden; 404 is the by-ID lookup pattern.
- "Already a 401": the key is valid, so authentication succeeds; 401 is only for unauthenticated requests.

excerpts.quote: The comparison never touches the database, so a 403 reveals nothing about /// whether the other workspace exists.
// Unauthenticated requests are rejected with 401 by the fallback policy. var user = context.HttpContext.User; if (user.Identity?.IsAuthenticated != true || user.GetWorkspaceId() == routeWorkspaceId)
A by-ID endpoint instead combines ID and the caller's workspace in its lookup, returning 404 for a resource outside that workspace.

readMore.why: The full reasoning for 403 on workspace routes and 404 on by-ID lookups.

items.title: One creation path, kept honest by parity tests, not the compiler
items.body:
The right answer: convention, guarded by ChannelParityTests and the ADR itself.

ADR 0009 funnels chat and email creation through `ConversationStarter.StartAsync` so every channel gets the same SLA stamping, auto-assignment, assignment event and webhooks. It is honest about the limit: nothing in the type system stops a future controller from creating a `Conversation` directly. What catches a divergent path is `ChannelParityTests`, which runs one scenario down both channels and asserts the same SLA, assignee and events, together with the ADR that states the rule.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "The compiler, via an internal constructor": the ADR says the compiler does not enforce the rule.
- "A Roslyn analyzer": none is mentioned; the guard rails are the tests and the ADR.
- "A database trigger": the start-time steps are application code committed in one save; no trigger checks them.

excerpts.quote: The parity tests and this ADR are the guard rails.

items.title: The timestamp is inside the signature, so it cannot be refreshed
items.body:
The right answer: the HMAC covers the timestamp too, and re-signing needs the secret.

Harbor does not sign the body alone. It signs the string `{timestamp}.{body}` with HMAC-SHA256 and sends the timestamp next to the signature. A receiver recomputes the HMAC over `{t}.{body}` with the shared secret, compares it, and rejects a `t` outside its tolerance window. If an attacker swaps in a fresh timestamp, the recomputed HMAC no longer matches the captured signature, and producing a new valid one needs the secret the attacker does not have.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Receivers use the HTTP Date header": the check uses the signed `t` value.
- "Receivers store every timestamp they have seen": the ADR's defence is the tolerance window plus the signature, not a store of seen values.
- "Deliveries are bound to Harbor's IP": the ADR mentions no IP binding.

excerpts.quote: the signature is still cryptographically valid, but the timestamp it covers is stale, and the attacker cannot re-stamp it without the secret.

items.title: Open, snoozed and closed add up to total; unassigned overlaps
items.body:
Every conversation is in exactly one state: open, snoozed or closed. So for one filtered population, those three counts add up to the total. "Unassigned" is a different question (does anyone own it?), not a fourth state. An unassigned conversation is also open, snoozed or closed, so it is already counted once. Adding unassigned to the sum would count those rows twice. The guide says this directly: `unassigned` overlaps the groups; do not add it to the total.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "All four add up to total": that double-counts unassigned conversations.
- "Each count ignores its own filter, like facets": the guide says the overview is not a set of facets; with `state=Open` the closed count is simply zero.
- "Total counts only the current page": the overview counts the whole filtered population without paging.

excerpts.quote: The overview counts the same filtered population without applying paging. Its `open + snoozed + closed` equals `total` for valid conversation states. `unassigned` overlaps these groups; do not add it to the total.
This endpoint is not a set of facets that each ignore their own filter.

items.title: A token on the round-robin pointer would reject customers
items.body:
The right answer: a token would 409 the save that commits a customer's new conversation.

The pointer bump is saved in the same SaveChanges as the new conversation. With a concurrency token, the second of two simultaneous arrivals would fail with DbUpdateConcurrencyException and a 409, and that failure would reject an incoming customer message just to keep the rotation fair. ADR 0006 decides rotation fairness is not a correctness property, so the pointer is an ordinary column whose concurrent update may be lost. The worst case is one teammate getting an extra conversation, which self-corrects.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "SQLite serializes the writes, so nothing is lost": the ADR calls this a classic lost update and ConcurrencyTests prove the loss happens silently.
- "The pointer is recomputed on read": it is a stored column, and the lost write does persist.
- "A token would deadlock": optimistic tokens take no locks; they fail the save.

excerpts.quote: Failing it to protect the pointer means rejecting an incoming customer message.

items.title: Why Paging casts page to long before multiplying
items.body:
An `int` holds values up to about 2.1 billion. `page` and `size` can each be valid ints, yet `(page - 1) * size` can be far bigger. If you do that sum in `int`, it wraps around and can even become negative. The debugging lab shows `page = int.MaxValue`, `size = 200` giving `-400`.

`Paging.cs` line 55 writes `((long)page - 1) * size`. The cast to `long` comes first, so the subtraction and multiplication happen in 64-bit math, which has room for the real answer. Then, if that offset is past the total, the helper returns an empty page; only a small, useful offset is cast back to `int` for `Skip`.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "checked arithmetic, let it be a 500": a huge page is valid input; Harbor clamps it to an empty page instead of failing.
- "multiply in int, then cast the product": the guide says `(long)((page - 1) * size)` only widens a result that may already be wrong.
- "multiply in int, reject negatives": a wrapped result is not always negative, and Harbor does not reject the request.

excerpts.quote: // Widen BEFORE multiplying: int.MaxValue is valid query-string input. // A wrapped negative offset could accidentally return the first page. var offset = ((long)page - 1) * size; if (offset >= total) { return []; }
The cast must happen **before** multiplication. `(long)((page - 1) * size)` only widens a result that may already be wrong.
The broken result is `-400`; the correct result is `429496729200`.

readMore.why: Lab 1 reproduces the old overflow in an isolated test.

items.title: Two endpoints agreeing does not mean either is right
items.body:
A parity test checks that the list endpoint and the overview endpoint give the same answer. That proves they are consistent with each other. It does not prove they are correct. The workshop's example: if both forget the `workspaceId` filter, both include rows from another tenant, so they still agree, while leaking another customer's data. The fix is to compare each endpoint to an independent expected set, add a foreign workspace row that otherwise matches the filter, and check totals too, since a count can leak even when no foreign row is returned.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Parity tests are flaky (different transactions)": the guide's objection is a missing check, not flakiness.
- "The overview rounds its counts": the overview returns plain counts; nothing in the guides mentions rounding.
- "Paging means totals never agree": the overview counts the same filtered population without paging, so totals can and should agree.

excerpts.quote: If list and overview both forget `workspaceId`, they might agree while leaking another tenant's data. Compare both to an independent expected set.
Check totals as well as returned IDs: aggregate data can leak without returning the foreign row.
The overview counts the same filtered population without applying paging.

items.title: Harbor finds a teammate by the digest of the presented key
items.body:
The right answer: the handler hashes the presented key with SHA-256 and looks up the teammate by that digest.

ADR 0001 stores only the SHA-256 digest of each key, in the unique column `Teammate.ApiKeyHash`. The plain key exists once, in the creation response, and never in the database. So authentication cannot compare plain keys; it hashes whatever the caller sent and searches for that digest. The matching teammate's id, workspace id and role become claims that the scope filter, role checks and request logging read.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Decrypt each stored key": hashing is one-way and nothing decryptable is stored.
- "Read the teammate id inside the key": a key is `hbk_` plus 48 generated hex characters; it encodes no teammate.
- "Compare the plain key with every stored key": there are no stored plain keys to compare with; the lookup is a single digest match.

excerpts.quote: `ApiKeyAuthenticationHandler` hashes the presented key and looks up the teammate by digest.

items.title: A parameter name that silently swallowed ?page=
items.body:
The right answer: it clashed with PageRequest.Page and silently ignored ?page=.

When the action parameter was declared as `[FromQuery] PageRequest page`, its name collided with the `Page` property of the same object, and the `?page=` value never reached it. Nothing errored: every request quietly got page one. The test suite missed it because every test asserted page one too. The fix was renaming the parameter to `paging`, and `PaginationBoundaryTests` now walks to a real second page on every list endpoint so the regression cannot return unnoticed.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "It failed to bind, so every call was a 400": the bug was silent; requests succeeded with the wrong page.
- "It shadowed a route value, so page 2 was a 404": no route value or 404 was involved.
- "It clashed with the X-Page header": the collision was with the object's own property, not a response header.

excerpts.quote: collided with the object's own `Page` property and silently ignored `?page=`, and every test passed because they all asserted page one.

items.title: Core idea: name the guarantee, then name what it cannot prevent
items.body:
The reliability and testing guides share one habit: never stop at "it works". Say exactly what is promised, and then say one thing that can still go wrong.

Practise it on the mechanisms these guides discuss:

- **Transactions.** List everything a given save writes, then ask which of those effects live in the database and which do not.
- **Version tokens.** Trace which request reads the version and which request sends it back, and ask over what window of time the check actually applies.
- **Tests.** The workshop gives a fill-in sentence for every test, ending with "It does not prove [limit]." Fill it in for one test before you read the next section.
- **Time.** Find how the domain methods learn the current time, and ask what that means for testing an exact deadline.

When you read a quiz in this pack, try to state the promise in one sentence and the remaining failure in another. That is the skill the guides want you to practise.

excerpts.quote: Goal: identify a system's actual guarantee and a failure it cannot prevent.
Use this pattern: “Given [fixture], when [operation], assert [observable result]. This catches [defect]. It does not prove [limit].”
Goal: choose a test by the defect it should catch.

items.title: Core idea: a request passes through stages, and each can reject it
items.body:
A web request does not jump straight into your controller code. In Harbor it passes through stages, in order:

1. **Identity.** The API key says who is calling (a teammate in some workspace). The guide stresses that a workspace GUID in the URL proves nothing about permission by itself.
2. **Binding and validation.** The query string is turned into a typed request object. Text that cannot become the right type, or a filter that breaks a simple rule, is rejected before the controller runs.
3. **Application coordination.** The controller builds a query and decides what to do with it.
4. **Persistence and response.** EF Core turns the query into SQL, runs it, and the controller writes the JSON and headers.

Why this matters: when something fails, the status code and the stage go together. Before you change code, ask which stage should own this failure. The guide's exercise is a table of bad inputs, each with the stage that rejects it and one test that shows it.

excerpts.quote: authorization failures and binding failures can short-circuit before the action.
The HTTP route identifies an operation. The API key identifies an authenticated teammate. A GUID in the URL is not proof of permission.
For each, write the stage that rejects it and one test that would establish the behavior.

Where the API key becomes teammate, role and workspace claims.

items.title: The 403/404 rule is inherited by construction and pinned by tests
items.body:
The right answer: one global filter and per-query scoping enforce it, and WorkspaceScopeMatrixTests pin it.

The workspace-scoped 403 lives in one global filter, `WorkspaceScopeFilter`, so any new route under `/api/workspaces/{workspaceId}/...` gets it automatically. The by-id 404 comes from the scoping predicate every resource query includes. Because the split can look inconsistent at a glance, the ADR pins it with a dedicated test class rather than trusting reviewers to remember.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Each controller checks by hand; code review pins it": the point of the design is that endpoints do not each re-implement the rule.
- "A middleware looks the workspace up per request": the scoped-route 403 is decided without touching the database.
- "Route attributes and the OpenAPI document": neither is mentioned; the mechanism is the filter plus the query predicate.

excerpts.quote: The rule is enforced in one global filter for scoped routes and one scoping predicate per resource query, so new endpoints inherit it by construction.

items.title: Harbor keys have no rotation or expiry; revoking is manual
items.body:
The right answer: delete or re-issue that teammate's credential by hand.

ADR 0001 is explicit about what the scheme lacks: there is no built-in key rotation and no expiry. Revoking a key means deleting or re-issuing the teammate's credential. The ADR accepts this for the current scope and notes a mitigating design point: because every request goes through a single lookup point, adding rotation later would be a local change.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Wait for built-in expiry": keys do not expire.
- "Call the rotation endpoint with a grace period": no rotation exists yet; a grace period would be part of a future design.
- "Revoke the bearer token at the OAuth server": bearer-token and OAuth flows were rejected as overkill for service-to-service traffic, so there is no token server.

excerpts.quote: There is no built-in key rotation or expiry; revoking a key means deleting or re-issuing the teammate's credential.

items.title: What an EnsureCreated test database cannot catch
items.body:
`EnsureCreated` builds the test database straight from today's EF model, the C# classes as they are right now. A real development database is built and upgraded by migrations, the step-by-step change scripts. If you add a property to a model but forget the migration, the tests still pass: their schema came from the model and already has the new column. An existing database never gets that column, and the app fails against it. That gap is why `MigrationDriftTests` exists as a separate guard. (The debugging labs include this exact symptom: tests pass but startup cannot find a column.)

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "Disables foreign-key checks": the workshop says nothing like this; its point is model vs migrations.
- "Switches to an in-memory provider": the factory uses real SQLite, one connection per test class.
- "Deletes rows after each test class": the workshop does not describe this; seed data is not the gap it names.

excerpts.quote: `HarborApiFactory` uses `EnsureCreated`, building schema from today's EF model. Development startup uses migrations. A model can pass the HTTP suite while missing a migration required by an existing database. Read `MigrationDriftTests` and explain why the separate guard exists.
one SQLite connection per test class and a fake webhook sender.

items.title: Count, then fetch: two statements, no snapshot
items.body:
`Paging.ToPageAsync` first runs `CountAsync` on the query and then, as a separate step, `Skip/Take/ToListAsync`. These are two separate SQL statements. Nothing holds the data still between them. If someone adds or closes a conversation in that gap, the count header and the page can disagree slightly. The guide's conclusion: that is fine for an interactive queue, but it is not an immutable export snapshot. When you truly need a frozen view, that is a different requirement.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "The page is fetched first": the code counts first, then fetches.
- "Total is computed from the page rows": the total comes from a database count of all matches; a page has at most `size` rows.
- "They always agree in one implicit transaction": the guide says they are separate statements and a writer between them can change the dataset.

excerpts.quote: The list first counts matches, then fetches a page. Those are separate statements, so a writer between them can change the dataset. The response is useful for an interactive queue; it is not an immutable export snapshot.
var total = await query.CountAsync(cancellationToken);
